meta.note: Static scenario bank. No network calls, no live data. Return figures are deliberately rounded ranges with a confidence field: the ranking of outcomes is what the game depends on and what is reliable, the exact percentages are approximate and marked as such. Entries tagged 'theory' have no real returns at all and are reasoned mechanisms.
meta.assetKeys: Each option carries a label and a move string. 'move' is a rounded range over the stated period unless noted.

scenarios.title: The mark becomes wallpaper
scenarios.setup: Germany is printing money to pay reparations and to fund a general strike in the occupied Ruhr. The central bank has no independence and is monetising government deficits directly. Prices are doubling every few weeks and workers are being paid twice a day so they can spend before the money loses value. Bank deposits still pay a nominal interest rate that looks generous.
scenarios.question: Where do you hold your wealth?

options.label: Cash and bank deposits in marks
options.move: Total loss, effectively -100%

options.label: German government bonds
options.move: Total loss in real terms, effectively -100%

options.label: Shares in German industrial companies
options.move: Severe real losses but survived, roughly -70% to -90% in real terms

options.label: Farmland, property, machinery, gold
options.move: Broadly preserved real value

options.label: Foreign currency, especially dollars
options.move: Preserved value and bought distressed German assets cheaply

scenarios.explanation: Hyperinflation is not a price problem, it is the destruction of the unit of account. Anything whose value is defined as a fixed number of marks goes to zero: cash, deposits, bonds, pensions, insurance policies, and any loan you were owed. Anything whose value is defined by what it is rather than what it is denominated in survives. Holding a foreign currency was strictly better than holding hard assets because it kept the optionality of buying real assets later at collapsed prices, which is exactly what foreign buyers did. German equities are the interesting case: shares represent claims on real productive assets, so in principle they should have been an inflation hedge, and in nominal terms they rose by absurd multiples. But in real terms they still lost most of their value, because the companies were operating in a collapsing economy with destroyed supply chains, and because equity holders were competing with a state seizing what it could.
scenarios.takeaway: In a currency collapse, sort every asset by one question: is its value written as a number of currency units, or is it a claim on something real? The first group goes to zero. The second group merely suffers.
scenarios.repeatability: Highly repeatable. Zimbabwe in 2008, Venezuela through the 2010s, Turkey and Argentina in milder form. The mechanism has never varied. What varies is whether foreign currency is legally holdable, which is the practical risk rather than the analytical one.

scenarios.title: Debt deflation
scenarios.setup: The equity market has just broken after a decade of margin-financed speculation. Banks are failing in waves and each failure destroys deposits, so the money supply is contracting sharply. Prices are falling, not rising. The dollar is pegged to gold, which means the Federal Reserve cannot ease aggressively without threatening the peg, and it raises rates in 1931 to defend it. Nominal debts are fixed while incomes and prices fall.
scenarios.question: Where do you put your money at the start of 1930?

options.label: US equities
options.move: Roughly -85% peak to trough by mid-1932

options.label: Corporate bonds
options.move: Investment grade held up, low grade fell hard with defaults

options.label: Long US Treasuries
options.move: Positive nominal returns, strongly positive real returns

options.label: Currency held outside the banking system
options.move: Strongly positive in real terms as prices fell around 25%

options.label: Physical gold
options.move: Fixed at $20.67 until 1933, then revalued to $35, around +69%

options.label: Property
options.move: Large nominal declines, widespread foreclosure

scenarios.explanation: This is the mirror image of Weimar and the single best illustration of why you cannot memorise asset rankings without understanding the mechanism. Under deflation, a fixed nominal claim becomes more valuable in real terms every month, so the assets that were annihilated in Germany were the winners in America. Long Treasuries gave you both the real gain from falling prices and a capital gain as yields fell, with no default risk. Cash was excellent in real terms but only if you held it outside a bank, because roughly a third of American banks failed and deposit insurance did not exist until 1933. Gold deserves a note: it looks like a winner because of the 1933 revaluation, but private gold holding was made illegal by executive order that same year and holders were compelled to sell at the old price, so the paper return was not generally capturable. That is a recurring feature of crises rather than a footnote: the state changes the rules precisely when your hedge is working.
scenarios.takeaway: Deflation rewards the highest quality nominal claim you can find and punishes leverage without mercy. The asset ranking is roughly the exact inverse of an inflationary crisis, which is why the regime is the question and the asset is only the answer.
scenarios.repeatability: The mechanism repeats whenever a credit bust is met with insufficient monetary response. Japan after 1990 is the long modern version. It did not repeat in 2008 or 2020 because central banks had learned this specific lesson and flooded the system, which is why those episodes rhymed with inflation rather than deflation.

scenarios.title: The gold window closes
scenarios.setup: The dollar has been convertible to gold at $35 an ounce since 1944, and every other major currency is pegged to the dollar. But the United States has been running deficits to fund both the Vietnam War and domestic expansion, and there are now far more dollars outstanding than there is gold at Fort Knox to back them. France and others begin presenting dollars for gold. In August 1971 Nixon suspends convertibility.
scenarios.question: You see the pressure building in early 1971. What do you own?

options.label: Gold
options.move: $35 to roughly $180 by end-1974, around +400%

options.label: Dollar cash
options.move: Devalued against gold, gold-backed currencies and later against everything

options.label: US equities
options.move: Flat to 1972, then roughly -45% in the 1973-74 bear market

options.label: Swiss franc and Deutsche mark
options.move: Substantial appreciation against the dollar

options.label: Broad commodities
options.move: Large gains, accelerating into the 1973 oil shock

scenarios.explanation: When a fixed price is defended by a shrinking reserve, the fixed price is the trade. Gold was pinned at $35 by policy, not by supply and demand, and everyone could see the reserves draining. That is an asymmetric position: the peg either holds and you lose nothing much, or it breaks and the price goes wherever the accumulated imbalance says it should. The subtler point is what the break unleashed. Ending convertibility removed the external constraint on US monetary policy, and the 1970s inflation followed directly. So gold was not only a trade on the devaluation, it was a trade on the entire decade that the devaluation made possible. Equities are the trap answer here: nominal GDP was about to grow enormously, which sounds good for stocks, but the multiple investors were willing to pay collapsed as inflation rose, and that de-rating overwhelmed the earnings growth.
scenarios.takeaway: A price held by policy against a draining reserve is not a price, it is a countdown. And when a monetary constraint is removed, ask what the constraint had been preventing, because that is the multi-year trade.
scenarios.repeatability: Every broken peg follows this shape: the ERM in 1992, the Thai baht in 1997, the Swiss franc ceiling in 2015. The reserve drains, officials deny, then the break is instant and large. Highly repeatable in structure, and the timing is always the hard part.

scenarios.title: The first oil shock
scenarios.setup: OPEC declares an embargo in response to Western support for Israel in the Yom Kippur War. The oil price quadruples in months. This is a supply shock, not a demand shock: it raises costs across the entire economy while simultaneously reducing output. Central banks face rising inflation and rising unemployment at the same time, and the policy consensus has no framework for that combination.
scenarios.question: Where do you allocate as the embargo begins?

options.label: Oil and energy producers
options.move: Strongly outperformed, though not immune to the broad bear market

options.label: Broad developed equities
options.move: Roughly -45% peak to trough in real terms, UK far worse

options.label: Long government bonds
options.move: Deeply negative real returns as inflation ran into double digits

options.label: Gold
options.move: Roughly doubled over 1973-1974

options.label: Short-dated cash
options.move: Negative real but far less bad than bonds or equities

options.label: Broad commodities
options.move: Strong gains across energy and industrials

scenarios.explanation: A supply shock has a structural feature worth internalising: the cost that is destroying every other business is revenue for someone. That makes the shock source the cleanest hedge available, because it is not merely uncorrelated with the damage, it is the mechanical other side of it. Gold worked for a different reason, as a hedge against the monetary consequence rather than the shock itself. Everything with a fixed nominal claim was destroyed, and equities were hit twice, once through margin compression as input costs rose and again through multiple compression as inflation raised the discount rate. Cash performed the unglamorous role it usually plays in a stagflation, losing slowly while everything else lost quickly. Note what does not work: the classic sixty-forty portfolio has no defence at all here, because stocks and bonds fall together when the shock is inflationary. That correlation flip is the single most important thing this episode teaches.
scenarios.takeaway: In a supply shock, own the shock. And remember that stocks and bonds diversify each other only when the dominant risk is growth. When the dominant risk is inflation, they move together and your diversification evaporates exactly when you need it.
scenarios.repeatability: Repeated closely in 2022, where energy was the only major sector up and sixty-forty had its worst year in generations. Highly repeatable, and the correlation lesson is the durable part.

scenarios.title: Volcker breaks the back of inflation
scenarios.setup: Inflation is running near 14% and has been high for a decade, so expectations of high inflation are now embedded in wage contracts and pricing behaviour. Paul Volcker takes over the Federal Reserve and announces that the money supply, not the interest rate, is the target. The Fed funds rate goes above 19%. A severe recession follows, unemployment reaches almost 11%, and the Fed does not blink.
scenarios.question: It is late 1981. Rates are at their peak, inflation is starting to turn, and everyone is certain inflation is permanent. Where do you put your money for the next five years?

options.label: Long US Treasuries at 15% yields
options.move: Start of a bull market that ran roughly forty years

options.label: Gold
options.move: Peaked in January 1980 and fell for two decades, roughly -60% by 1999

options.label: US equities
options.move: Bottomed in August 1982, then a generational bull market

options.label: Cash at 15%
options.move: Excellent while it lasted, then reinvestment at ever lower rates

options.label: Commodities
options.move: Long bear market through the 1980s and 1990s

scenarios.explanation: This is the most valuable scenario in the bank because it is where following the previous decade's playbook cost you the most. Everything that had worked from 1971 to 1980 was gold, commodities and real assets, and every one of them was about to enter a twenty-year bear market. The reason is that asset prices are set against expectations, not against levels. A 15% bond yield with inflation about to fall to 4% is one of the great asymmetric trades in financial history, and it was available precisely because nobody believed inflation could be beaten. Cash is the instructive near-miss: 15% risk free felt obviously correct and it paid beautifully for two years, but it carried enormous reinvestment risk, because when rates fell you had to roll into 8%, then 6%, then 4%, while the bondholder had locked the high rate in for thirty years. Choosing cash over long bonds is failing to distinguish a yield you receive today from a yield you have secured.
scenarios.takeaway: The best trade usually requires believing the consensus regime is about to end, which is why it is available. And when rates peak, duration is the trade: locking a high yield beats receiving a high yield.
scenarios.repeatability: The specific trade requires a credible central bank breaking an inflation, which is rare. The general lesson, that peak rates plus peak pessimism on inflation favours long duration, is broadly applicable and was worth acting on again in late 2023.

scenarios.title: The Plaza Accord
scenarios.setup: Volcker's high rates have pulled enormous capital into the dollar and it has appreciated roughly 50% against major currencies. American manufacturing is being hollowed out by the exchange rate and Congress is drafting protectionist legislation. In September 1985 the finance ministers of the US, Japan, West Germany, France and the UK meet at the Plaza Hotel and agree to coordinate intervention to push the dollar down.
scenarios.question: You read the communiqué on the Monday morning. What do you do?

options.label: Short the dollar, long the yen
options.move: Dollar fell roughly 50% against the yen over two years

options.label: Japanese equities
options.move: Roughly tripled into the 1989 peak

options.label: US equities
options.move: Strong until the October 1987 crash, then recovered

options.label: Stay long dollars
options.move: Large losses in any other currency's terms

options.label: Gold
options.move: Rose moderately as the dollar weakened

scenarios.explanation: The rare case where the authorities announce the trade in advance and you are simply asked whether you believe them. What made it credible was that the coordinating governments wanted the same outcome for domestic political reasons, so the intervention had genuine commitment behind it rather than being one central bank leaning against a market. The consequence chain matters more than the trade. Japan cut rates and eased aggressively to offset the damage a strong yen did to its exporters, and that easing inflated the greatest asset bubble of the twentieth century in Japanese land and equities. So the highest-returning position was not the currency but the second-order effect: Japanese assets, floated on the liquidity created to fight the currency move you had already predicted.
scenarios.takeaway: When a policy move is coordinated and politically wanted by all parties, take it at face value. Then ask what each country will do to offset the pain, because the offsetting policy is usually the bigger trade.
scenarios.repeatability: Coordinated intervention on this scale has not recurred, and unilateral intervention usually fails. Low repeatability for the trade. The habit of asking what the offsetting policy will be is permanently useful.

scenarios.title: Black Monday
scenarios.setup: Equities have run up strongly for five years. Portfolio insurance strategies are widely used: they mechanically sell index futures as the market falls, in order to synthetically replicate a put option. Rates have been rising and there is friction over the dollar. On 19 October 1987 the Dow falls 22.6% in a single session, the largest one-day percentage decline in its history. The economy, however, is not in recession and corporate earnings are fine.
scenarios.question: It is the close on Black Monday. What do you do with cash you were holding?

options.label: Buy equities aggressively
options.move: Fully recovered within two years, strong long-run returns

options.label: Stay in cash and wait for clarity
options.move: Missed the recovery, safe but costly

options.label: Buy long Treasuries
options.move: Sharp rally on the flight to quality, then gave much of it back

options.label: Buy gold
options.move: Brief spike, no sustained trend

options.label: Short equities into the panic
options.move: Badly wrong, the reversal was fast

scenarios.explanation: The essential question in any crash is whether the price is telling you something about cash flows or something about market plumbing. In 1987 there was no recession, no credit event and no earnings collapse. What there was, was a feedback loop: portfolio insurance sold futures as prices fell, that selling pushed prices lower, which triggered more programmatic selling, into a market whose specialists ran out of capital to absorb it. That is a liquidity event, and liquidity events mean revert because the selling is mechanical and finite rather than informed. Contrast this with 1929 or 2008, where the price decline was correctly telling you that the credit system and the earnings base were broken. The discipline is to ask what is actually being sold and by whom, and whether the seller is choosing to sell or being forced to. Forced sellers create opportunity, informed sellers create warnings.
scenarios.takeaway: Distinguish a plumbing crash from a solvency crash. If the selling is mechanical and the economy is intact, violent declines are opportunities. If the selling reflects a real deterioration in credit or earnings, they are only the beginning.
scenarios.repeatability: The pattern repeats regularly, most cleanly in the 2010 flash crash, February 2018 volmageddon, and the March 2020 liquidity phase. Very repeatable, but so is the failure mode of misreading a solvency crisis as a plumbing crisis.

scenarios.title: The bubble that never came back
scenarios.setup: Japanese equities trade near sixty times earnings and Tokyo land is valued so highly that the grounds of the Imperial Palace are said to be worth more than California. Banks lend against property collateral, and property is collateral for equity purchases. The Bank of Japan starts raising rates in 1989 to deflate the bubble. In 1990 the market turns. Corporate balance sheets are deeply levered against collateral that is now falling.
scenarios.question: It is 1992. The Nikkei has already halved from its peak and looks cheap against its own history. Where do you put your money for the next decade?

options.label: Japanese equities
options.move: Fell for another eleven years, roughly -80% peak to 2003 trough

options.label: Japanese government bonds
options.move: Yields fell from around 5% toward zero, sustained strong returns

options.label: Japanese property
options.move: Fell for roughly fifteen consecutive years

options.label: US equities
options.move: One of the strongest decades in history to 2000

options.label: Yen cash
options.move: Near zero nominal return but positive real as prices fell

scenarios.explanation: After a debt-financed asset bubble bursts, companies stop trying to maximise profit and start trying to repair their balance sheets. They pay down debt even when borrowing is nearly free, because they are insolvent on a mark-to-market basis and know it. That is why cutting rates to zero did not restart credit growth: the problem was not the price of credit but the willingness to take any. In that world, the demand for money to invest keeps falling, so bond yields keep falling, and the government bond of a country with a large domestic savings base becomes an excellent multi-decade asset even at yields that look absurdly low. Two traps here. The first is valuation: halved from a bubble peak was still expensive, and cheap relative to its own bubble history is not cheap. The second is the assumption that zero rates must be inflationary, which is a claim about the supply of money and ignores the demand for credit.
scenarios.takeaway: A balance sheet recession is not a monetary policy problem, and normal valuation anchors do not apply after a bubble. When the private sector is deleveraging, own the highest quality duration you can and be extremely sceptical of anything priced against the bubble era.
scenarios.repeatability: Directly informed the response to 2008 and 2020, where authorities deliberately recapitalised the system fast to avoid exactly this outcome. So the episode is instructive but the policy response has changed, which is why 2008 did not become a fifteen-year deflation.

scenarios.title: Sterling leaves the ERM
scenarios.setup: The UK has joined the European Exchange Rate Mechanism at what many consider too high a rate against the Deutsche mark. Britain is in recession and needs lower rates. Germany, dealing with the inflationary cost of reunification, is running tight policy and will not cut. The peg requires the UK to match German tightness while its own economy contracts. Reserves are being spent defending the rate and the Treasury raises the base rate to 15% in a single day.
scenarios.question: You watch the base rate go to 15% to defend the peg. What is the position?

options.label: Short sterling against the mark
options.move: Sterling fell roughly 15% within weeks of the exit

options.label: Long gilts
options.move: Strong rally once the peg broke and rates could finally fall

options.label: UK equities
options.move: Strong multi-year recovery after the exit

options.label: Buy sterling, trust the Treasury
options.move: Immediate large loss

scenarios.explanation: A peg is a promise, and a promise is only as good as the willingness to pay its cost. Here the cost was keeping a recessionary economy at German interest rates indefinitely, and no elected government pays that price forever. That makes the position asymmetric in a very specific way: if the peg holds you lose the carry, which is small and known, and if it breaks you make the whole devaluation, which is large. You are effectively buying a cheap option from a government that has told you the strike. The genuinely useful part is the aftermath. Leaving the ERM was treated as a national humiliation, and it was followed by fifteen years of solid British growth, because the exit permitted the monetary policy the economy actually needed. Gilts and UK equities both rallied hard. The event everyone called a catastrophe was the removal of the constraint that was causing the damage.
scenarios.takeaway: Find the trade where the authority has publicly committed to something its own electorate will not tolerate. And separate the humiliation of breaking a commitment from the economics of being free of it, because markets reliably confuse the two.
scenarios.repeatability: Structurally very repeatable and the same logic worked on the Thai baht in 1997 and the Swiss franc ceiling in 2015. The euro removed the mechanism within Europe by abolishing the pegs, which is why the 2011 crisis expressed itself in bond spreads instead.

scenarios.title: The Asian crisis
scenarios.setup: Thailand, Indonesia, South Korea and Malaysia have grown fast on foreign capital. Local banks and corporates have borrowed in dollars at low rates and lent in local currency, because the currencies are pegged to the dollar so the mismatch looks free. Current account deficits are widening. Thailand's reserves come under pressure and in July 1997 the baht is floated. It falls sharply, and every dollar debt in the region suddenly costs far more in local currency terms.
scenarios.question: The baht has just been floated. Where do you position?

options.label: Short regional currencies and equities
options.move: Indonesian rupiah fell around 80%, regional equities down 60% to 85%

options.label: Buy the dip in Asian equities
options.move: Far further to fall before the 1998 bottom

options.label: Dollars and US Treasuries
options.move: Strong, dollar rose and Treasuries rallied on the flight to quality

options.label: Oil
options.move: Fell hard as Asian demand collapsed, to around $10 by end-1998

options.label: Gold
options.move: Fell, dollar strength dominated the crisis-hedge bid

scenarios.explanation: Currency mismatch is the most reliably lethal structure in finance. Borrowing in a hard currency to fund local currency assets is profitable for as long as the peg holds, and it converts a devaluation from a competitiveness adjustment into a solvency event, because your liabilities reprice upward while your assets do not. That is why the usual textbook logic, that a weaker currency helps exporters, failed completely: the borrowers were bankrupt before the export benefit could arrive. Two secondary lessons. Contagion spread not because the economies were similar but because the same foreign investors owned all of them and had to raise cash, which is a positioning channel rather than a fundamental one. And gold is the instructive failure: this was a crisis in which the safe-haven asset fell, because the crisis was a scramble for dollars specifically, not a loss of faith in money. Knowing which kind of crisis you are in decides whether gold or dollars is the hedge.
scenarios.takeaway: Look for hard-currency debt funding local-currency assets, and treat the resulting devaluation as a solvency event rather than a trade adjustment. In a dollar-shortage crisis the dollar is the haven, not gold.
scenarios.repeatability: Highly repeatable and it recurred in Russia 1998, Argentina 2001, and in milder form in Turkey. The 2020 dollar squeeze had the same signature until the Fed opened swap lines, which is now the standard circuit breaker.

scenarios.title: The dotcom unwind
scenarios.setup: The Nasdaq has roughly tripled in eighteen months. Companies with no earnings are valued on page views and on their spending rate, and the argument that traditional valuation no longer applies is widely accepted by serious people. The Fed has been raising rates through 1999 and into 2000. Meanwhile so-called old economy assets, energy, industrials, value stocks and real estate, are deeply out of favour and cheap.
scenarios.question: It is March 2000. Where do you put your money for the next three years?

options.label: Technology and telecoms
options.move: Nasdaq fell roughly 78% to the 2002 trough

options.label: Value and old economy equities
options.move: Modestly positive to flat while growth collapsed

options.label: REITs and property
options.move: Strongly positive through the downturn

options.label: US Treasuries
options.move: Strong as the Fed cut from 6.5% to 1%

options.label: Gold
options.move: Bottomed in 2001 and began a decade-long bull market

options.label: Cash
options.move: Positive nominal, comfortably ahead of equities

scenarios.explanation: The dominant feature of this unwind is that it was a valuation event rather than an economic catastrophe. The 2001 recession was mild and short. What collapsed was the price people would pay for a dollar of future earnings, and that collapse was concentrated in the assets where the price had been most extreme. That is why the correct answer is not simply defensive but specifically anti-correlated with the bubble: Treasuries as the Fed cut hard, and real assets that had been starved of capital while everything flowed into technology. There is a broader mechanism worth naming. A bubble does not only misprice its own sector, it starves the rest of the economy of capital, which suppresses supply and sets up the next cycle's winners. Almost no capital went into oil exploration, mining or housing in the late 1990s, and those were the great trades of 2003 to 2008. The other side of every mania is a capital drought somewhere else.
scenarios.takeaway: When a mania breaks, the best positions are usually whatever the mania was starving of capital, not merely whatever is defensive. And a valuation unwind can be brutal for prices while barely touching the real economy.
scenarios.repeatability: The capital-drought mechanism is highly repeatable and explains the 2022 energy trade after a decade of underinvestment. The mildness of the recession is not a general rule and depended on there being no large credit component.

scenarios.title: The global financial crisis
scenarios.setup: US house prices have been falling since 2006. Mortgages were securitised into structures rated triple-A on the assumption that regional housing markets do not fall together, and banks hold these at high leverage with short-term funding. Bear Stearns fails in March 2008 and is rescued. In September, Lehman Brothers is allowed to fail, money market funds break, and the short-term funding market for the entire banking system stops.
scenarios.question: It is September 2008, the week Lehman fails. What do you own?

options.label: US Treasuries
options.move: Strongly positive, the clearest winner of 2008

options.label: Dollar cash
options.move: Appreciated sharply as global funding scrambled for dollars

options.label: Global equities
options.move: Roughly -50% peak to the March 2009 trough

options.label: Corporate and high yield credit
options.move: Severe losses in 2008, then a historic rally through 2009

options.label: Gold
options.move: Fell during the acute deleveraging, then rose strongly from 2009

options.label: Commodities
options.move: Oil fell from around $145 to near $35

scenarios.explanation: In an acute deleveraging, correlations converge to one and almost nothing diversifies, because the selling is driven by margin calls rather than by views. Levered holders must raise cash, so they sell whatever they own, including the assets that should be hedges. That is precisely why gold fell during the worst months and only worked later, once the policy response created the inflation and debasement concerns it actually hedges. The winners were the two assets you can settle obligations in: Treasuries and dollars. The most valuable part of this episode is the timing distinction. The right answer in September 2008 was Treasuries and cash, and the right answer in March 2009 was credit and equities, six months apart and diametrically opposed. Credit in particular offered equity-like returns with a senior claim once the government had guaranteed the funding markets. The regime changed when policy changed, and reading the policy response was worth more than reading the economy.
scenarios.takeaway: In a forced deleveraging, own the settlement asset and expect every correlation to fail. Then watch policy, because the moment the funding backstop appears, the whole ranking inverts and the best risk-adjusted trade is usually senior in the capital structure.
scenarios.repeatability: The March 2020 crash followed the identical two-phase script at ten times the speed. Extremely repeatable, and knowing that phase two exists is the difference between surviving and profiting.

scenarios.title: The euro crisis
scenarios.setup: Greece has revealed its deficit is far larger than reported. Because eurozone members share a currency, they cannot devalue or print, so a fiscal problem becomes a solvency problem, and bond markets begin pricing default risk in Portugal, Ireland, Spain and Italy. Italian ten-year yields pass 7%. Banks across Europe hold their own sovereign's debt, so the sovereign and the banks threaten each other. Breakup of the euro is openly discussed.
scenarios.question: It is July 2012. Italian and Spanish yields are at crisis levels and Draghi has just said the ECB will do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. What do you do?

options.label: Buy Italian and Spanish government bonds
options.move: Yields collapsed over the following two years, very large returns

options.label: Stay in German Bunds
options.move: Safe but gave up the entire spread compression

options.label: European bank equities
options.move: Sharp rally from the 2012 lows, though a poor long-run holding

options.label: Short the euro
options.move: Wrong on the immediate move, the euro strengthened into 2014

options.label: Gold
options.move: Peaked in 2011 and fell hard through 2013

scenarios.explanation: A central bank that can print the currency a debt is denominated in can always prevent a liquidity-driven default in that debt. The eurozone periphery was priced for default because investors were unsure whether the ECB regarded Italian debt as its responsibility. Once Draghi made clear that it did, the default premium was not slowly negotiated away, it was mostly removed by the statement, because the risk had been about willingness rather than capacity all along. The discipline this teaches is to separate a solvency problem from a coordination problem. Greece was genuinely insolvent and did restructure with large private losses. Italy was solvent but illiquid, and it was priced as though it were Greece. Buying the illiquid solvent borrower once the lender of last resort declares itself is one of the highest reward-to-risk trades that recurs in markets, and it also required going against the entire narrative of the previous two years.
scenarios.takeaway: Ask whether the borrower is insolvent or merely without a lender of last resort. When a central bank credibly commits to being that lender, the risk premium disappears with the statement rather than with the fundamentals.
scenarios.repeatability: Repeated in March 2020 when the ECB's pandemic programme did the same for the same bonds, and in the 2023 US regional bank episode where the funding backstop stopped the run within days. Highly repeatable.

scenarios.title: The taper tantrum
scenarios.setup: The Fed has been buying bonds for years and the economy is recovering slowly with inflation below target. In May 2013 Bernanke mentions that the pace of purchases may be reduced in coming months. He is not raising rates and not selling anything. Ten-year Treasury yields rise from around 1.6% to around 3% over the following months. Capital that had flowed into emerging markets seeking yield begins reversing.
scenarios.question: Yields are moving sharply on nothing but a signal about future purchases. Where is the damage?

options.label: Emerging market currencies and local debt
options.move: Heavy losses, worst in high current account deficit countries

options.label: Long US Treasuries
options.move: Negative, one of the worst years in decades for duration

options.label: Gold
options.move: Roughly -28% in 2013, its worst year in a generation

options.label: US equities
options.move: Up roughly 30% in 2013, largely unaffected

options.label: REITs and other yield proxies
options.move: Fell notably as real yields rose

scenarios.explanation: Two lessons sit inside this episode. First, the marginal price of an asset is set by the marginal buyer, and if that buyer is there for yield rather than for the asset itself, the asset is not exposed to its own fundamentals, it is exposed to the yield gap. Emerging market local debt had not become riskier in May 2013, but the reason people owned it had disappeared. The countries that broke were those needing continuous foreign inflows to fund current account deficits, which is a funding vulnerability rather than a valuation one. Second, and this is the part most people get backwards, US equities rose 30% in the year that duration was destroyed. Tapering was a signal of a strengthening economy, which is good for earnings and bad for bonds. Whether rising yields hurt equities depends entirely on why yields are rising: growth-driven rate rises are usually fine for stocks, inflation-driven rate rises are not. That distinction separates 2013 from 2022.
scenarios.takeaway: Ask why the marginal holder owns the asset, because that is what they are actually exposed to. And when yields rise, diagnose the cause before assuming equities suffer: growth-driven increases and inflation-driven increases have opposite implications.
scenarios.repeatability: The reach-for-yield unwind repeats whenever policy tightens, and the same emerging market vulnerability screen worked again in 2015, 2018 and 2022. Highly repeatable.

scenarios.title: China devalues
scenarios.setup: China's growth is slowing after a vast credit-financed investment boom, and the yuan has been effectively pegged upward against a strengthening dollar, which is tightening Chinese monetary conditions at the wrong moment. In August 2015 the PBOC devalues the yuan by around 2% and shifts the fixing mechanism. Capital flight accelerates and reserves fall by hundreds of billions. Commodity markets, which had built enormous supply to serve Chinese construction, face the prospect of that demand disappearing.
scenarios.question: The yuan has just been devalued. Where do you position for the next twelve months?

options.label: Short industrial commodities and mining equities
options.move: Iron ore, copper and oil fell hard into early 2016

options.label: Short commodity-exporting emerging markets
options.move: Heavy losses in Brazil, South Africa, Australia and Canada

options.label: Long US Treasuries
options.move: Strong as global deflation fears pushed yields to new lows

options.label: US equities
options.move: Two sharp corrections but roughly flat over the period

options.label: Gold
options.move: Bottomed in December 2015 and rallied strongly through 2016

scenarios.explanation: When a very large economy devalues, it exports deflation to everyone who competes with it or sells to it. The specific mechanism here was that a decade of Chinese fixed asset investment had pulled enormous supply into existence across mining and heavy industry, and that supply was sized for demand that was structurally ending rather than cyclically pausing. Excess capacity meeting falling demand is the classic setup for a commodity bear market, and it takes years to clear because mines and mills have long lives and high shutdown costs. The elegant part is the chain: the devaluation hit commodity prices, commodity prices hit the exporting countries' currencies and equity markets, and the resulting global disinflation pushed developed market bond yields to record lows and forced the Fed to postpone its own tightening. One devaluation in Beijing set the interest rate in Frankfurt.
scenarios.takeaway: Trace who supplies the devaluing economy and who competes with it, because that is where the price moves. And distinguish excess capacity from a demand dip: capacity built for demand that is not coming back takes years to clear, which makes the bear market long rather than sharp.
scenarios.repeatability: The deflation-export mechanism is very repeatable for any large economy that devalues. The specific commodity supercycle unwind was a once-in-a-generation scale event tied to Chinese urbanisation.

scenarios.title: The pandemic crash and the reflation
scenarios.setup: A novel virus forces economies to shut down deliberately. Equities fall roughly 34% in five weeks, the fastest bear market on record, and even Treasuries sell off briefly as levered funds liquidate everything for cash. Then the response arrives at a scale with no precedent: the Fed cuts to zero, buys corporate bonds for the first time, and opens dollar swap lines globally, while governments send money directly to households rather than only to banks.
scenarios.question: It is late March 2020. The Fed has just announced it will buy corporate bonds and Congress is passing direct payments to households. What do you do?

options.label: Buy equities and credit aggressively
options.move: Equities recovered to new highs within five months

options.label: Hold cash until the virus is understood
options.move: Missed one of the fastest recoveries on record

options.label: Long Treasuries
options.move: Good in the crash, poor from mid-2020 as reflation took hold

options.label: Commodities and real assets
options.move: Bottomed in 2020 then rose powerfully through 2021 and 2022

options.label: Gold
options.move: Strong through mid-2020, then flat as real yields rose

scenarios.explanation: The crash phase was a repeat of 2008's plumbing failure, compressed into weeks, and it was resolved the same way, by a central bank becoming the buyer of last resort. Buying corporate bonds directly was the decisive line, because it removed the possibility of a solvency cascade among otherwise viable companies. Once that guarantee existed, the risk that had been priced no longer existed, and the recovery was correspondingly violent. But the more important and more missed part is what the fiscal response set up. Previous crises pushed money into the banking system, where it sat as reserves and inflated asset prices without raising consumer prices. In 2020 money went directly to households while supply chains were physically constrained, which is demand meeting restricted supply, and that is the actual definition of inflation. The 2021 to 2022 inflation was visible in the design of the March 2020 policy response, roughly eighteen months before it appeared in the data, and it made real assets the trade of the following two years rather than the bonds that had won every previous crisis.
scenarios.takeaway: Separate the crash from the response. And look closely at where policy money is delivered: into bank reserves it inflates assets, into household bank accounts against constrained supply it inflates prices. The delivery mechanism, not the size, determines the regime that follows.
scenarios.repeatability: The crash-then-backstop script is highly repeatable. The direct fiscal transfer was novel, and its inflationary consequence is the main reason authorities are now more cautious about repeating it.

scenarios.title: Inflation is not transitory
scenarios.setup: Inflation is rising fast, and central banks describe it as transitory, caused by supply chains and base effects. Policy rates remain at zero and bond buying continues into 2022. Bonds yield close to nothing, so a lot of capital has been pushed into long duration equities whose value depends on cash flows far in the future. Then Russia invades Ukraine and energy and food prices spike on top of the existing pressure.
scenarios.question: It is late 2021. Inflation is at multi-decade highs and central banks are still at zero. Where do you put your money?

options.label: Energy producers and commodities
options.move: Energy was the standout winner, up strongly in 2022

options.label: Long duration growth and technology
options.move: Severe losses, unprofitable technology down 60% to 80%

options.label: Long government bonds
options.move: Worst year for developed duration in modern records

options.label: A classic sixty-forty portfolio
options.move: Both legs fell together, worst year in generations

options.label: Short-dated cash
options.move: Negative real but strongly outperformed both stocks and bonds

options.label: Value, banks and defensives
options.move: Modest losses, large outperformance versus growth

scenarios.explanation: The 1973 lesson repeated almost exactly, which is the point of having both in the bank. Own the shock: energy was the source of the inflation and therefore the beneficiary. But two structural features deserve attention. First, the correlation between stocks and bonds is not a constant, it is a function of what the dominant macro risk is. For the four decades of falling inflation, bonds rallied whenever equities fell, because the shared driver was growth. When the shared driver became inflation, both fell together, and every risk model calibrated on the previous era understated portfolio risk badly. Second, duration is not a bond concept. A company whose cash flows arrive in fifteen years is a long duration asset, and when the discount rate rises its present value falls just as a thirty-year bond's does. Investors who thought they had diversified out of interest rate risk by selling bonds and buying growth technology had in fact concentrated it. Cash as the runner-up is the honest answer for a year in which the correct answer for most portfolios was simply owning less of everything.
scenarios.takeaway: Stock-bond diversification depends on inflation being contained; when inflation is the dominant risk, they are the same trade. And duration is about when cash flows arrive, not about which asset class the label says it is.
scenarios.repeatability: The mechanism is fully repeatable and matches 1973 to 1974 closely. The specific magnitude reflected starting from zero yields, which left duration with no cushion at all.

scenarios.title: A bank run at internet speed
scenarios.setup: After a year of rapid rate rises, banks that took in large deposits during 2020 and 2021 and invested them in long-dated Treasuries and mortgage bonds are sitting on large unrealised losses. Those holdings are not marked to market on the balance sheet. Silicon Valley Bank has an unusually concentrated depositor base of venture-backed companies, mostly above the insurance limit, who talk to each other constantly. Word spreads and the bank loses a quarter of its deposits in a day.
scenarios.question: SVB has failed and regional bank shares are collapsing. Where do you position?

options.label: Short regional banks
options.move: Correct and profitable, the sector stayed impaired

options.label: Long short-dated Treasuries
options.move: Sharp rally as rate expectations were repriced hard

options.label: Large cap technology
options.move: Rallied strongly for the rest of 2023

options.label: Gold
options.move: Rose to near record highs within weeks

options.label: Large money centre banks
options.move: Gained deposits from fleeing regionals, outperformed regionals

scenarios.explanation: The tempting answer is to short the banks, which was correct but modest. The far larger move came from the second-order effect. A banking scare forced the market to price rate cuts, real yields fell, and the assets most sensitive to the discount rate were large cap technology, which then rallied for the rest of the year. So a crisis in banking produced its biggest returns in an unrelated sector, through the rates channel. Two further points. The failure was not credit, it was duration: the bonds were Treasuries and would have paid in full if held, but the bank had funded thirty-year assets with deposits that could leave in an afternoon, which is a maturity mismatch. And the run was faster than any in history because depositors were concentrated, digitally connected and mostly uninsured, which is a reminder that market structure changes the speed and therefore the survivability of old risks. The authorities guaranteed the deposits and the panic stopped in days, which is the 2012 Draghi lesson applied to banks.
scenarios.takeaway: Trace the second-order channel, because a shock in one sector usually pays best somewhere else through rates. And distinguish a duration mismatch from a credit problem: the assets can be perfect and the bank can still fail.
scenarios.repeatability: Maturity mismatch causing runs is as old as banking and entirely repeatable. The speed is new and getting faster. The backstop response is now the standard playbook, which shortens these episodes considerably.

scenarios.title: Telling a supply shock from a demand shock
scenarios.setup: Inflation is rising to 6% and the central bank must respond. You are told only one additional fact: output and employment are also falling. No specific country, no date.
scenarios.question: What does this combination tell you, and what does it imply for assets?

options.label: A supply shock: costs up, output down, and central banks face a genuine trade-off
options.move: Correct diagnosis

options.label: A demand shock: too much spending chasing available goods
options.move: Inconsistent with falling output

options.label: Purely a monetary phenomenon, unrelated to real activity
options.move: Incomplete, ignores the output signal

options.label: A measurement artefact that will pass on its own
options.move: The transitory argument, and the standard error

scenarios.explanation: The diagnostic is the co-movement of prices and output. In a demand shock, prices and output move together: too much spending raises both, and tightening policy reduces both, so the central bank faces no dilemma and its job is easy. In a supply shock, prices and output move in opposite directions, and now there is a real trade-off, because the tool that reduces inflation also deepens the output decline. This is why stagflation is analytically hard rather than merely unpleasant. For assets, the implications are sharp. A demand shock means bonds fall while equity earnings hold up, and the classic diversified portfolio survives. A supply shock means equities are hit through margins and through the discount rate simultaneously, bonds are hit through inflation, and the only reliable positions are the shock source itself, broad real assets, and short-dated cash. This single distinction explains almost every asset allocation outcome in 1973, 2022, and the 2020 to 2021 sequence in which a supply constraint met a demand stimulus.
scenarios.takeaway: Look at prices and output together, not at prices alone. Same direction means demand and a manageable problem. Opposite directions means supply, a policy trade-off, and no shelter in a conventional portfolio.
scenarios.repeatability: This is a definition rather than an episode, so it always applies. The practical difficulty is that real shocks are usually mixtures, and the honest question is which component dominates.

scenarios.title: What the yield curve is actually saying
scenarios.setup: The two-year government bond yields more than the ten-year, an inversion that has preceded most recessions of the last fifty years. Equity markets are at highs, unemployment is low and credit spreads are tight. No date, no country.
scenarios.question: What is the curve telling you, and what usually happens next?

options.label: The market expects policy rates to be lower in future, which means it expects the economy to weaken
options.move: Correct reading

options.label: The market expects lower long-run inflation and nothing more
options.move: Part of the story, insufficient alone

options.label: A recession is already underway
options.move: Usually early, the lag has historically been long and variable

options.label: A technical distortion with no macro content
options.move: The usual dismissal, and usually wrong

scenarios.explanation: A long bond yield is roughly the average of expected short rates over its life, plus a term premium. So when the ten-year sits below the two-year, the market is saying it expects short rates to be cut, and central banks cut when the economy is deteriorating. That is the whole signal, and it is a statement about expectations, not a causal mechanism. Two things people get wrong. First the lag: inversion has often preceded recession by twelve to twenty-four months, and equities have frequently made their highs after the inversion, so treating it as a sell signal has been expensive. Second the mechanism: an inverted curve is also directly damaging rather than merely predictive, because banks fund short and lend long, so inversion compresses the profitability of lending and tightens credit supply. The signal and the cause overlap. And it can be wrong for a good reason, if term premium or foreign demand for long bonds distorts the long end, which is why it should be read alongside credit spreads and lending standards rather than alone.
scenarios.takeaway: Read the curve as an expectation of future policy rates, which is an expectation about growth. Respect it as a signal, distrust it as a timing tool, and remember it also causes tightening rather than only forecasting it.
scenarios.repeatability: The signal has a strong record but a small sample, perhaps eight or nine cycles, so confidence should be moderate rather than high. It has produced at least one prominent false alarm, and it should never be the only input.

scenarios.title: Why gold sometimes ignores inflation
scenarios.setup: Inflation is running at 7%. Gold, supposedly the classic inflation hedge, is flat to lower. In a different period, inflation is at 2% and gold is rising strongly. No dates given.
scenarios.question: What actually drives gold?

options.label: Real interest rates: the return on the safe alternative to holding it
options.move: The dominant driver

options.label: The inflation rate itself
options.move: Only through its effect on real rates

options.label: Crisis and fear
options.move: Real but episodic and often overwhelmed by real rates

options.label: The dollar alone
options.move: Correlated, but mostly a mirror of the same real rate driver

scenarios.explanation: Gold pays no cash flow, so the cost of holding it is whatever a safe asset would have paid you in real terms. When real yields are deeply negative, that cost is negative and gold is attractive. When a central bank raises nominal rates faster than inflation and real yields turn positive, holding a non-yielding asset becomes genuinely expensive and gold struggles even while inflation is high. This resolves the apparent contradiction: gold is not a hedge against inflation, it is a hedge against inflation that the central bank is not responding to, and those are different things. The same framework explains the crisis behaviour. Gold usually falls in the acute phase of a deleveraging, because levered holders sell everything for cash, and then rises afterwards, because the policy response drives real yields down. It also clarifies which crisis it hedges: a loss of confidence in money is a gold event, whereas a scramble for dollars to settle dollar obligations is a dollar event, and gold can fall in the second.
scenarios.takeaway: Price gold off real yields, not off inflation. It hedges unaddressed inflation and monetary debasement, not the CPI print, and in a dollar funding squeeze it is not the haven at all.
scenarios.repeatability: The real rate relationship is robust across decades, with genuine exceptions when central bank buying or an acute crisis bid dominates for a period.

scenarios.title: The most dangerous structure in finance
scenarios.setup: A fast-growing country has a currency pegged to the dollar. Local banks borrow dollars cheaply abroad and lend in local currency at higher rates, pocketing the spread. Everyone points out that the peg has held for a decade and the carry has been excellent. The current account deficit is widening.
scenarios.question: What is the risk, and what happens when the peg breaks?

options.label: Liabilities reprice upward while assets do not, so devaluation becomes a solvency event
options.move: Correct

options.label: A devaluation would help, by making exports cheaper
options.move: The textbook answer, and wrong when debt is mismatched

options.label: The main consequence is imported inflation
options.move: True but secondary to the balance sheet damage

options.label: Contained, since the borrowers are hedged by their local assets
options.move: The assumption that fails, they are not hedged at all

scenarios.explanation: This structure profits steadily and then fails catastrophically, which is exactly the payoff profile that accumulates the most of it before breaking. The carry looks like free money for as long as the peg holds, so the position grows until it is systemically large. When the currency falls 40%, dollar liabilities rise 40% in local terms while local currency assets do not move, and borrowers who were profitable become insolvent overnight. That is why the standard competitiveness argument fails here: a cheaper currency does help exporters, but only if they survive long enough to sell anything, and the banking system that finances them has already failed. The screening rule that comes out of this is concrete: find entities whose liabilities are in a currency they do not earn. That single question would have flagged Asia in 1997, Russia in 1998, Argentina in 2001, and a good deal of what strains emerging markets whenever the dollar rises sharply.
scenarios.takeaway: Hunt for liabilities denominated in a currency the borrower does not earn. A long-standing peg is not evidence of safety, it is the reason the position got large enough to matter.
scenarios.repeatability: Extremely repeatable and it is one of the few genuinely reliable screens in macro. The mechanism has never changed, only the geography.

scenarios.title: Who is selling, and do they want to?
scenarios.setup: An asset falls 30% in two weeks. Nothing has changed in its earnings, its credit quality or its industry. Volume is enormous.
scenarios.question: What do you need to establish before deciding whether this is an opportunity?

options.label: Whether the sellers are choosing to sell or being forced to
options.move: The decisive question

options.label: Whether it is cheap on historical multiples
options.move: Useful but insufficient, and misleading after a bubble

options.label: Whether it has found technical support
options.move: Not a claim about the mechanism

options.label: Whether there is news explaining it
options.move: Often absent precisely in mechanical selling

scenarios.explanation: Forced selling and informed selling look identical on a price chart and mean opposite things. A margin call, a fund redemption, an index rebalance, a risk limit breach and a mechanical hedging programme all generate selling that carries no information about value, and it is finite, because once the position is liquidated the selling stops. Informed selling carries information and is not finite in the same way, because it reflects a reassessment that others will also make. So the practical work is to identify the seller's constraint: who owned this, why did they own it, what would force them out, and how much is left to sell. That framework explains why 1987 was a buy and 1929 was not, why credit in early 2009 was a generational opportunity, and why the March 2020 Treasury sell-off was bizarre and short lived. It also tells you why valuation alone is a weak tool here: after a bubble, an asset can be down 50% and still expensive, so cheapness relative to its own recent history is nearly worthless as a signal.
scenarios.takeaway: Identify the seller and the constraint. Mechanical selling is finite and creates opportunity, informed selling is a warning, and the price alone cannot tell you which you are looking at.
scenarios.repeatability: Always applicable and one of the highest-value habits in markets. The difficulty is that the information about who is being forced out is often only visible after the fact.

scenarios.title: Where the money is delivered
scenarios.setup: Two countries respond to a downturn with the same headline amount of stimulus, say 15% of GDP. Country A does it through central bank purchases of government bonds from banks. Country B sends the money directly to households as transfers, while goods are in short supply.
scenarios.question: What differs in the outcome?

options.label: Country A inflates asset prices, Country B inflates consumer prices
options.move: The core distinction

options.label: Broadly the same, since the money supply rises equally
options.move: Ignores who receives it and what they do with it

options.label: Neither is inflationary if the output gap is large
options.move: True only while supply can respond

options.label: Country B is simply more effective with no trade-off
options.move: More effective at supporting demand, with an inflation cost

scenarios.explanation: Quantitative easing swaps one financial asset for another inside the financial system. It raises bank reserves and lowers yields, which pushes investors along the risk curve and lifts asset prices, but it does not by itself put spending power in the hands of anyone who buys goods. That is why a decade of large-scale asset purchases after 2008 produced asset price inflation and persistent worry about consumer price inflation that never arrived. Direct transfers are categorically different, because the recipient spends on goods and services. If supply can expand, you get output rather than inflation. If supply is constrained, as it was physically in 2020 and 2021, you get prices. This is the single most useful frame for understanding why the same nominal stimulus produced no inflation in one decade and a great deal of it in the next, and it also explains the distributional politics: the first channel raises the value of assets, which are held by the already wealthy, while the second raises incomes.
scenarios.takeaway: Ask who receives the money and what they buy with it. Into the financial system it lifts asset prices. Into households against constrained supply it lifts consumer prices. Size matters much less than the delivery channel.
scenarios.repeatability: The distinction held clearly across the 2008 and 2020 responses and is now a mainstream part of policy debate. It is a strong framework rather than a precise law.

scenarios.title: The other side of every mania
scenarios.setup: One sector has attracted overwhelming investor enthusiasm for the better part of a decade. Capital is nearly free for anyone operating in it. Meanwhile a capital-intensive, unglamorous industry has been starved: no new mines, wells, refineries or shipyards have been financed, and existing operators have been rewarded by markets for cutting investment and returning cash instead.
scenarios.question: Where is the next cycle's return likely to come from, and why?

options.label: The starved industry, because supply cannot respond when demand recovers
options.move: The capital cycle answer

options.label: The favoured sector, since capital follows opportunity
options.move: Usually already in the price

options.label: Neither, sector returns are unpredictable
options.move: Ignores an observable supply constraint

options.label: Bonds, since a mania unwind means recession
options.move: Depends entirely on whether inflation is the constraint

scenarios.explanation: Returns in capital-intensive industries are driven less by demand than by supply, because demand tends to grow smoothly while supply arrives in enormous lumps after long delays. A copper mine takes roughly a decade from discovery to production, so if no mines were financed for eight years, no amount of price signal creates supply next year. That inelasticity is exactly what produces violent price moves and high returns for incumbents. The capital cycle framework says to look for industries where capital has been leaving, capacity is being retired, and the surviving operators are consolidated and disciplined, then wait for any demand recovery to meet a supply base that cannot respond. This is why energy was the best performing sector of 2022 after a decade of disinvestment, and why shipping, uranium and fertiliser have all had violent cycles from the same setup. The symmetry matters too: the favoured sector's problem is that free capital invites competitors, and abundant capital destroys returns just as reliably as scarce capital creates them.
scenarios.takeaway: Follow the capital, not the story. Industries starved of investment develop inelastic supply, which creates the next cycle's returns, while industries flooded with capital compete their own returns away.
scenarios.repeatability: One of the more reliable frameworks in equity investing, with a good record across commodities, shipping and semiconductors. Timing is the persistent weakness, since droughts can last far longer than expected.

scenarios.title: Illiquid or insolvent
scenarios.setup: A borrower's bonds are trading at distressed levels. Its debt is denominated in a currency it does not control. There is a large central bank in the system, but it has not said whether this borrower falls within its responsibility.
scenarios.question: What determines whether this is a buying opportunity?

options.label: Whether the borrower is fundamentally solvent and whether a lender of last resort will declare itself
options.move: The two questions that matter

options.label: Whether the yield compensates for the historical default rate
options.move: Assumes the distribution is stationary, which it is not in a run

options.label: Debt to GDP and the primary balance alone
options.move: Necessary but not sufficient without the funding question

options.label: Distressed sovereign debt is never worth the risk
options.move: Has been among the best risk-adjusted trades when the backstop arrives

scenarios.explanation: Default has two entirely different causes and they demand opposite trades. An insolvent borrower cannot pay under any plausible circumstances, and buying its debt cheaply is simply taking a loss more slowly. An illiquid but solvent borrower can pay if it can refinance, and its problem is that nobody will lend during a panic, which is self-fulfilling: the fear of default raises the yield, the higher yield makes default more likely. That loop can only be broken by a lender willing to lend when nobody else will, and that is precisely what a central bank is for. The critical asymmetry is that a central bank that can create the currency the debt is written in faces no limit on its capacity, only on its willingness. So the trade is not a bet on fundamentals improving, it is a bet on an institution accepting a responsibility. When that acceptance is announced credibly, the risk premium collapses immediately rather than gradually, which is why these trades pay so much so quickly and why waiting for confirmation in the fundamentals means missing them entirely.
scenarios.takeaway: Separate cannot pay from cannot refinance. For the second, the entire question is whether a lender of last resort exists and will act, and that is a question about institutional willingness rather than about arithmetic.
scenarios.repeatability: Highly repeatable, with 2012 in Europe, 2020 globally and 2023 in US regional banking all following the same shape. The failure mode is misjudging genuine insolvency as illiquidity, which is what happened to holders of Greek debt.

scenarios.title: Positioning is the risk, not the news
scenarios.setup: A macro condition has persisted for so long that it is treated as structural rather than cyclical. Institutions have rebuilt themselves around it: benchmarks, risk models, product design and career incentives all assume it continues. Nothing in the data currently contradicts it.
scenarios.question: What does that tell you about the distribution of returns from here?

options.label: The payoff is asymmetric against the consensus, because the continuation is fully priced and the reversal is not
options.move: The core insight

options.label: The trend is well established, so following it is the higher probability trade
options.move: Higher probability, poor expected value if the price already assumes it

options.label: Nothing, since positioning is unobservable
options.move: Partly true, but it is inferable from prices and product flows

options.label: A reversal is imminent
options.move: The timing error that ruins the insight

scenarios.explanation: Asset prices embed expectations, so what you earn depends on the difference between what happens and what was already assumed, not on what happens. When a regime has lasted long enough to become an assumption, the price of its continuation is high and the price of its reversal is low, which creates asymmetry regardless of which is more likely. Long bonds in 1981 are the cleanest example: everyone knew inflation was permanent, so a 15% yield was available, and that yield was payment for taking the unpopular side. Japanese equities in 1989 were the reverse, priced for permanent growth. Two disciplines are needed to use this without being destroyed by it. First, high probability and good expected value are different things, and the consensus is usually right about the next quarter and badly wrong about the next decade. Second, and this is where most people lose money with a correct thesis, the asymmetry says nothing about timing. Regimes persist for years after they become fragile, so the position has to be sized to survive being early, which usually means buying the cheap option rather than shorting the expensive consensus.
scenarios.takeaway: The more thoroughly a regime is assumed, the better the payoff for the other side and the worse the payoff for agreeing. Size for being early, because the asymmetry tells you about the distribution and nothing at all about the date.
scenarios.repeatability: The principle is general and durable. Its practical application is genuinely difficult, and most of the people who identify a fragile regime correctly still lose money by being early with too much size.
